title: English for Today — Classes Nine and Ten
notes: User-accessible Drive textbook: grade verified from cover and parent folder; edition checked on PDF p.3; table of contents p.5. Scanned PDF, OCR used only as a reading aid; cited literary page images visually checked. PDF page equals printed page plus five for these works.

All 112 questions and suggested answers in this file are assistant-authored textbook-based practice, NOT verbatim NCTB exercises, board questions, school exam questions or official keys. No exam year, board or school provenance assigned. Require teacher review. Literary interpretations are not the only acceptable answers.

Fourteen distinct work-focused practice groups: seven poems; seven story/episode groups. The three Merchant of Venice episodes are adaptations of ONE play, not three distinct original works. Purple Jar parts are one combined set. No combinatorial copies to reach numerical targets.

Question-bank references store authored question wording, not invented passages. Original full works are not inserted as fabricated passages. Textbook file/checksum, work/author and exact PDF/printed page ranges remain available for verification.

Mr. Moti cause of death is unspecified in the excerpt. Girl’s accusations, gender roles and folk remedies are character speech, not endorsed guidance. No generalisations about religious/ethnic communities in the Merchant adaptation. Doctors’ joy explanation in Story of an Hour is narratively ironic, not a verified clinical cause. Solitude is not a factual rule that friends always abandon people. Literary water emergency response recommends professional help, not child entry into dangerous water.

questions.text: In “O Me! O Life!”, why does the speaker include himself among the foolish and faithless?
questions.answer: He reproaches his own failings as well as those he sees around him. This self-criticism prevents his complaint from being merely an attack on other people.

questions.text: What contrast is created by the long complaint and the short answer in Whitman’s poem?
questions.answer: The long complaint accumulates disappointment, while the brief answer offers a simple affirmation: life and personal identity exist, and each person can contribute.

questions.text: How does the image of a “powerful play” change the mood of “O Me! O Life!”?
questions.answer: It changes the emphasis from apparently useless struggle to ongoing participation. The individual can have a meaningful part in a larger shared existence.

questions.text: Why can “contribute a verse” be read as a metaphor rather than a demand that everyone write poetry?
questions.answer: A verse represents an individual contribution to the continuing play of life. It can stand for meaningful action or creativity, not only a literal written poem.

questions.text: What does the repeated address “O me! O life!” reveal about the speaker’s state of mind?
questions.answer: It gives the questioning an urgent, personal quality. The speaker is emotionally involved in the search for meaning rather than discussing it at a distance.

questions.text: How does “the struggle ever renew’d” suggest persistence as well as frustration?
questions.answer: The struggle is tiring because it returns, but its renewal also shows continued effort. The final answer suggests that participating remains worthwhile despite imperfect results.

questions.text: What does “identity” add to the answer in Whitman’s poem?
questions.answer: It affirms the existence of a particular person, not just life in the abstract. The individual’s presence makes a distinctive contribution possible.

questions.text: Does Whitman’s answer claim that every difficulty has disappeared? Explain from the ending.
questions.answer: No. The answer does not remove foolishness or struggle. It gives a reason to live and contribute while the larger play continues.

questions.text: In “Books”, how do new people enter the reader’s experience?
questions.answer: Opening a book brings imagined people into the reader’s thoughts and awareness. The poem says they rise in the reader’s fancies and eyes.

questions.text: What does the melting room in Farjeon’s poem suggest about attention?
questions.answer: The reader becomes so absorbed that the immediate room fades from awareness. The image describes imaginative absorption, not a physical change in the room.

questions.text: How can a character become a “chosen friend” in “Books”?
questions.answer: A reader can grow familiar with and care about a character while reading. This imagined companionship helps make the book personally meaningful.

questions.text: What kinds of distance can readers cross by sailing “along the page”?
questions.answer: They can imagine travelling to another country or to another period of history. Reading crosses distance in place and time without physical travel.

questions.text: Why does Farjeon place the body in a chair and the mind elsewhere?
questions.answer: The contrast distinguishes physical stillness from imaginative movement. Reading can make an outwardly quiet activity inwardly adventurous.

questions.text: What action unlocks the box in Farjeon’s metaphor?
questions.answer: A child’s touch, understood as opening and engaging with the book, unlocks the experiences within. The metaphor presents reading as accessible and full of possibility.

questions.text: How do the closing covers of a book differ from what they contain in “Books”?
questions.answer: The covers enclose a small physical object, but the words within can suggest many people, ideas, places and ages. The imaginative contents seem much larger than the object.

questions.text: Why is wonder a suitable description of the reading experience in Farjeon’s poem?
questions.answer: Books introduce unexpected ideas, imagined companions and unfamiliar worlds. These possibilities explain the opening celebration of books as worlds of wonder.

questions.text: Why should the “two Mothers” not be understood as two unrelated people?
questions.answer: The poem describes the same mother before and after a major change in her mental abilities. The apparent difference records the daughter’s experience of that change.

questions.text: What does the speaker inherit from her first mother besides affection?
questions.answer: She bears her mother’s physical features and facial expressions, and remembers the example her mother set. The inheritance is both bodily and emotional.

questions.text: How does the image of a clouded mind explain the change in the mother?
questions.answer: It suggests that her mental clarity has become obscured. The poem does not name a specific medical diagnosis, so one should not be invented.

questions.text: Why does the mother seem like a stranger although she still looks familiar?
questions.answer: Her appearance remains recognisable, but her changed mind and dependence alter how the daughter experiences their relationship.

questions.text: How does the daughter become her mother’s “strength”?
questions.answer: She takes on the supporting role that her mother once held. The change reverses their earlier relationship of care without ending their love.

questions.text: What does the circle image connect in Duncanson’s poem?
questions.answer: It connects the mother’s earlier care, the daughter’s present responsibility and the possibility that the daughter will one day need care herself.

questions.text: Why does the speaker refer to her own children near the end?
questions.answer: She asks them to continue the same loving care if she changes in old age. Her request is grounded in what she herself has tried to do for her mother.

questions.text: Does the poem suggest that a person becomes less worthy of love when dependent?
questions.answer: No. The speaker insists on loving both versions of her mother. Dependence changes the form of care required, not the person’s worth.

questions.text: How does the repeated instruction to call the cattle prepare us for Mary’s journey?
questions.answer: It establishes the ordinary task that sends her across the sands. Repetition gives the command a memorable rhythm that later becomes tragic.

questions.text: What is the effect of placing Mary alone against the wild western wind?
questions.answer: Her isolation makes her vulnerability more apparent. The powerful weather contrasts with a single person carrying out a routine task.

questions.text: How do the rising tide and descending mist work together in “The Sands of Dee”?
questions.answer: The tide spreads over the sands while the mist hides the land. Together they remove the safe, visible route home.

questions.text: Why is the line saying Mary never returned home a turning point?
questions.answer: It changes the account from an errand into a tragedy. The later discovery at sea confirms the loss that the line announces.

questions.text: What does the question about weed, fish or floating hair reveal?
questions.answer: It dramatises the observers’ uncertain recognition of a body in the water. The image of golden hair makes the discovery personal and distressing.

questions.text: How is the foam personified near the end of Kingsley’s poem?
questions.answer: It is described as cruel and hungry, as if it had intention and appetite. This personification gives the sea a threatening character.

questions.text: Why is the cattle call heard again after Mary’s burial?
questions.answer: Its return keeps the memory of Mary and her unfinished errand alive. It can be read as a haunting poetic echo rather than proof of a literal supernatural event.

questions.text: What responsible response could a reader suggest if witnessing an emergency like Mary’s?
questions.answer: Call emergency help, alert responsible adults and trained rescuers, and stay away from dangerous water. The poem should not be used to encourage an untrained child to enter a strong tide.

questions.text: How does Hodgson turn an abstract idea into someone who can be addressed?
questions.answer: He personifies Time as a travelling old man with a caravan and a jennet. The speaker can therefore invite, question and bargain with Time.

questions.text: Why does the invitation to become a guest imply a wish to pause time?
questions.answer: A guest stays for a while, whereas the travelling figure is always moving. Asking Time to stop for a day expresses the wish to hold a passing moment.

questions.text: What does offering silver bells and a golden ring reveal about the speaker?
questions.answer: The valuable gifts show how strongly the speaker desires a pause. Material wealth is imagined as a possible bargain, although the poem never shows Time accepting.

questions.text: How do flowers, singing children and bowing peacocks shape the welcome offered to Time?
questions.answer: They make the invitation festive, beautiful and elaborate. The imagined ceremony expresses the effort people would make to delay Time.

questions.text: Why does the poem move from Babylon and Rome towards cities not yet born?
questions.answer: The movement extends Time’s journey across civilisations, from the historical past towards an unknown future. Individual cities cannot contain that movement.

questions.text: What do the womb and tomb images suggest about cities?
questions.answer: They present cities as if they have lives: some are not yet born, while others will eventually disappear. Human settlements change within the larger movement of time.

questions.text: How does the repeated request in the final stanza affect the poem?
questions.answer: The request returns without a recorded acceptance. Its repetition emphasises enduring human desire rather than success in stopping Time.

questions.text: Should the travelling figure be treated as a factual description of an ethnic community?
questions.answer: No. It is a literary personification within the poem’s historical vocabulary. It should not be turned into a stereotype about real communities.

items.work: Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening
items.author: Robert Frost

questions.text: What does the speaker believe about the owner’s location in Frost’s poem?
questions.answer: He thinks the owner lives in the village and will not see him stopping. This makes the pause feel private and removed from ordinary social observation.

questions.text: Why might the absence of a farmhouse make the stop unusual for the horse?
questions.answer: There is no obvious practical destination or shelter nearby. The horse’s imagined surprise highlights that the speaker has stopped simply to look at the snowy woods.

questions.text: What sounds interrupt or define the quiet scene in Frost’s poem?
questions.answer: The harness bells briefly interrupt it, while the sweep of gentle wind and falling snow forms the remaining soundscape.

questions.text: How does the horse’s bell introduce a question without spoken dialogue?
questions.answer: The speaker interprets the shake as asking whether there has been a mistake. This personifies the horse and creates a contrast with the speaker’s absorbed attention.

questions.text: What tension does “But” introduce after the description of the woods?
questions.answer: It opposes the attraction of the woods to promises and responsibilities. The speaker recognises reasons to continue rather than remain in the beautiful setting.

questions.text: Why should an answer not name a specific destination or promise as a fact?
questions.answer: The poem does not identify either one. A reader may suggest a possibility, but it must be marked as interpretation rather than supplied information.

questions.text: How can the repeated final line carry both a literal and a reflective meaning?
questions.answer: Literally, the traveller still has distance to cover before resting. Reflectively, the line may suggest continuing duties or a longer journey through life.

questions.text: What is the effect of the rhyme pattern AABA BBCB CCDC DDDD?
questions.answer: The linked rhymes carry sound forward between stanzas, while the final repeated rhyme gives a strong sense of closure. This supports both movement and the weight of the ending.

questions.text: How does the opposition between singing and sighing develop the argument of “Solitude”?
questions.answer: Songs receive answering echoes, while sighs vanish. As a poetic contrast, this suggests that happiness attracts a response more readily than private sorrow.

questions.text: What human behaviour is suggested by crowded feasts and the world passing a fast?
questions.answer: People readily gather for enjoyment but may avoid deprivation and suffering. The contrast criticises conditional companionship rather than prescribing it.

questions.text: How do nectar and gall function as contrasting images in Wilcox’s poem?
questions.answer: Nectar suggests life’s sweetness or pleasure, while gall suggests bitterness or pain. The poem contrasts easily shared pleasure with suffering that can feel solitary.

questions.text: What difference is drawn between help in living and help in dying?
questions.answer: Generosity and companionship can support life, but no one can undergo another person’s death for them. This does not mean that care at the end of life is worthless.

questions.text: What does the image of narrow aisles add to the description of pain?
questions.answer: It suggests that people face suffering individually, one by one. The narrowness contrasts with the spacious, crowded halls of pleasure.

questions.text: Does “Solitude” require a reader to abandon a sad friend? Explain.
questions.answer: No. It describes a bleak pattern of behaviour; it is not an ethical instruction to repeat it. A reader may respond by valuing faithful support during hardship.

questions.text: How could someone reasonably disagree with the poem’s broad claim about friendship?
questions.answer: They could point to friends, family or carers who remain present during grief. Such an answer recognises the poem’s emotional force without treating it as a universal rule.

questions.text: How do the poem’s repeated contrasts organise its message?
questions.answer: Laughter and tears, song and sigh, feasting and fasting, and pleasure and pain form parallel oppositions. Together they make its account of social joy and private suffering memorable.

questions.text: How old is Ameen when he announces his decision to go to war?
questions.answer: He is seventeen. The announcement makes Sonabhan recognise both his growing independence and the possibility of losing his presence at home.

questions.text: What reassurance does Ameen offer his mother after supper?
questions.answer: He says that it will not take long and that he will return after training. The reassurance does not remove Sonabhan’s worry.

questions.text: What does Ameen’s silence at breakfast show about his awareness of Sonabhan?
questions.answer: He notices her puffy eyes and avoids raising the previous night’s subject. His silence suggests awareness of her distress, though the excerpt does not directly state all his thoughts.

questions.text: Which things has Sonabhan arranged for Ameen to sell at the market?
questions.answer: She has arranged two dozen eggs, a sheaf of areca nuts and a bottle gourd. These details locate the family’s daily life in a rural market economy.

questions.text: How do the neighbours’ complaints complicate Sonabhan’s view of her son?
questions.answer: They remind her of his mischievous behaviour and the trouble he has caused. Her apologising and offering eggs also show her continued protective affection.

questions.text: Why does Sonabhan refuse payment from the boys who want Moti for a fight?
questions.answer: She calls Moti her son and refuses to lend him. The response shows that she values the rooster as a loved presence, not merely as an animal that can earn money.

questions.text: What can the selected “Mr. Moti” excerpt establish about the cause of the rooster’s death?
questions.answer: It establishes that he is found cold and lifeless, but does not explain how he died. Naming a killer or a specific cause would go beyond the supplied excerpt.

questions.text: How do repeated images of emptiness convey Sonabhan’s loss after the burial?
questions.answer: The empty yard, veranda, home and bed connect physical surroundings with grief. The unopened doors and neglected daily routine show how deeply the loss affects her.

questions.text: How does the continuous chain of instructions shape the voice in “Girl”?
questions.answer: It creates a forceful, insistent voice that leaves little space for the listener. The form itself suggests the pressure of constant guidance and judgement.

questions.text: What difference is made between washing white and coloured clothes in “Girl”?
questions.answer: White clothes are assigned to Monday and the stone heap, while coloured clothes are assigned to Tuesday and the clothesline. These concrete rules establish the domestic setting.

questions.text: What does the girl’s brief denial about singing reveal about her position?
questions.answer: She tries to correct an accusation, but the stream of instructions continues. Her limited interruption shows how little control she has over the conversation.

questions.text: How do the directions for different kinds of smiles link domestic training to public behaviour?
questions.answer: They teach the girl how to manage different social relationships as well as household work. The instructions extend control from practical tasks to personal presentation.

questions.text: Why does the prohibition on playing marbles matter to the story’s treatment of gender?
questions.answer: The speaker explicitly says that the girl is not a boy. This shows a social rule about suitable behaviour, not evidence that girls are naturally unable to play.

questions.text: What tension exists between practical teaching and accusations in Kincaid’s story?
questions.answer: The speaker passes on useful household skills but also judges the girl’s character harshly. A reading can acknowledge concern without approving the insulting language.

questions.text: How does the bread question at the end show the gap between the two voices?
questions.answer: The girl asks about a practical obstacle, but the speaker treats it as another reason to judge what sort of woman she will become. Their concerns are not the same.

questions.text: Should the speaker’s advice in “Girl” be presented as modern medical or moral instruction?
questions.answer: No. It is the speech of a literary character within a particular social setting. Claims about cures, superstition and gender roles require critical reading, not automatic endorsement.

items.work: The Purple Jar — choice and consequences
items.author: Maria Edgeworth

questions.text: What does Rosamond’s reaction to unfamiliar shop goods reveal at the beginning?
questions.answer: She wants many attractive objects before knowing their names or uses. Her attention is led by appearance rather than an assessment of need.

questions.text: Why does the mother distinguish an attractive jar from a suitable flower pot?
questions.answer: She asks Rosamond to consider an object’s purpose, not merely its colour. The distinction challenges the assumption that wanting something makes it useful.

questions.text: How does the stone in Rosamond’s shoe change the shopping discussion?
questions.answer: It brings attention to a real practical need. The damaged shoe makes the choice between new shoes and an attractive jar consequential.

questions.text: Why is the jar’s purple appearance misleading?
questions.answer: The colour comes from the liquid inside rather than the glass. Emptying it reveals that Rosamond has bought something different from what she imagined.

questions.text: What opportunity for careful judgement does Rosamond miss before purchasing the jar?
questions.answer: Her mother asks her to examine it carefully, but excitement leads her to buy without checking the contents. The discovery at home follows from that haste.

questions.text: How does keeping to the agreed choice teach Rosamond about a limited budget?
questions.answer: The same money cannot buy both desired objects. Living with the consequences helps her see that choosing one purchase means giving up another.

questions.text: Why is Rosamond’s later inability to go out important to the lesson?
questions.answer: It makes the practical cost of neglecting her shoes visible in daily life. Her disappointment is more instructive than the jar’s loss of colour alone.

questions.text: How can a reader evaluate Rosamond’s mother without assuming there is only one acceptable judgement?
questions.answer: A reader may value her attempt to teach independent judgement while questioning whether the consequences are too severe. A reasoned answer should use details from the story.

items.work: The Merchant of Venice — A Pound of Flesh
items.author: William Shakespeare (textbook adaptation)

questions.text: How does the opening description explain why Antonio cannot immediately provide cash?
questions.answer: His wealth is tied up in merchandise carried by ships that are still at sea. Being wealthy does not mean he has the required cash available at that moment.

questions.text: What is Bassanio’s financial reason for asking Antonio for help?
questions.answer: He wants to visit Portia suitably equipped but lacks money because of his extravagant way of life. He turns to his generous friend for assistance.

questions.text: What contrast between Antonio and Shylock does the adaptation establish through lending?
questions.answer: Antonio is presented as helping people without interest, whereas Shylock lends for interest. The adaptation uses this conflict to explain their hostility; it should not become a generalisation about religious communities.

questions.text: Why is the penalty in the bond more dangerous than an ordinary repayment condition?
questions.answer: It threatens Antonio’s body and life if repayment is late. It creates a severe risk that cannot be measured simply as money.

questions.text: Why does Antonio believe signing the bond will be safe?
questions.answer: He expects his ships to return with valuable goods in time to repay the loan. The judgement depends on uncertain future events.

questions.text: How does concern for Bassanio influence Antonio’s choice?
questions.answer: His readiness to help his friend leads him to accept a personal risk. The episode presents loyalty alongside the danger of overconfidence.

questions.text: What amount and period are specified for the loan in the adapted episode?
questions.answer: The loan is three thousand ducats for three months. The dangerous flesh penalty is linked to failure to repay within the agreed time.

questions.text: Why should readers distinguish this adapted account from the whole play?
questions.answer: A textbook adaptation selects and simplifies events and character presentation. Answers about this excerpt should not silently import later developments or claim to describe every aspect of Shakespeare’s play.

items.work: The Merchant of Venice — The Three Caskets
items.author: William Shakespeare (textbook adaptation)

questions.text: What problem does Portia’s father try to address through the caskets?
questions.answer: He wants to choose a suitable husband and fears that a suitor may be attracted only by wealth. The test controls who may marry her even after his death.

questions.text: Why is choosing the gold casket not the same as choosing the most valuable relationship?
questions.answer: The test separates outward richness from the desired portrait. A precious exterior does not guarantee that the choice is wise.

questions.text: What does the Prince of Morocco’s reasoning reveal about appearances?
questions.answer: He associates Portia’s value with the richest material and therefore chooses gold. The outcome challenges that reliance on external splendour.

questions.text: How does the silver choice differ from Bassanio’s lead choice?
questions.answer: The silver choice depends on the prince’s belief that he deserves the best. Bassanio instead rejects impressive appearances and chooses the plain lead casket; this adaptation does not reproduce a lead inscription about giving and risking everything.

questions.text: Why is the lead casket central to the contrast between appearance and reality?
questions.answer: Its plain exterior is least impressive, but it contains the portrait that marks the successful choice. The result reverses an obvious ranking by material value.

questions.text: How does the marriage after Bassanio’s choice connect the test to Portia’s future?
questions.answer: Finding her portrait leads to their marriage. The test is therefore not merely a puzzle: its result decides who will become Portia’s husband under her father’s arrangement.

questions.text: What brings anxiety into the happiness following Bassanio’s success?
questions.answer: News arrives about Antonio’s financial danger and the threatened penalty. The change connects the marriage plot to the bond plot.

questions.text: Does the casket test establish that plain objects are always better in real life?
questions.answer: No. It is a designed literary test about judgement, value and commitment. Its symbolism should not be converted into a universal rule about material objects.

items.work: The Merchant of Venice — The Trial
items.author: William Shakespeare (textbook adaptation)

questions.text: Why is the Duke concerned even though a lawyer has been expected?
questions.answer: The bond appears legally binding, and the expected lawyer reports being ill. The Duke is unsure whether the young substitute can save Antonio.

questions.text: What roles do Portia and her companion adopt to enter the court?
questions.answer: Portia appears as Doctor Balthazar, a young lawyer, while her companion appears as a clerk. Their disguises allow them to take part in the legal proceedings.

questions.text: How does Portia first try to resolve the conflict without exploiting the bond’s wording?
questions.answer: She appeals to Shylock’s mercy and asks him to accept repayment. This attempts reconciliation before the technical legal argument.

questions.text: Why does Bassanio’s offer of extra money fail to settle the dispute?
questions.answer: Shylock insists on the stipulated penalty rather than financial compensation. His refusal shifts attention from repayment to the desire to enforce the bond.

questions.text: Why does Shylock initially praise the disguised Portia?
questions.answer: He believes her acknowledgement of his legal claim supports his demand. He has not yet recognised the limitation she will identify in the wording.

questions.text: What crucial distinction does Portia draw between flesh and blood?
questions.answer: The bond names a pound of flesh but grants no right to shed blood. In the adapted story, this makes carrying out the penalty impossible without incurring another penalty.

questions.text: How is Shylock’s movement towards Antonio interrupted?
questions.answer: As he approaches with a knife, Portia stops him and explains the blood restriction. The interruption turns apparent victory into defeat.

questions.text: What limitation should an answer observe when discussing the outcome of this adaptation?
questions.answer: The textbook episode ends with Antonio saved and Shylock leaving defeated. It should not be treated as a complete account of the original play’s legal proceedings or as real legal advice.

questions.text: Why does Richards believe the report about Brently Mallard at first?
questions.answer: He sees Brently’s name in the newspaper office’s report of a railway disaster and seeks confirmation by a second telegram. Despite that apparent checking, the report proves wrong.

questions.text: How does Mrs. Mallard’s immediate weeping complicate a claim that she never cared for her husband?
questions.answer: Her spontaneous grief shows that her response is not simply delight at his supposed death. The later feeling of freedom exists alongside genuine and complicated emotion.

questions.text: What do the open window and signs of spring suggest as Louise sits alone?
questions.answer: They suggest life, possibility and an opening beyond the limits she has felt. This is a symbolic reading supported by the new growth, fresh air and patches of blue sky.

questions.text: Why is Louise initially afraid of the feeling that approaches her?
questions.answer: She has not yet named it and seems to resist its implications. Recognising personal freedom after news of a death conflicts with what she may be expected to feel.

questions.text: How can the husband be described as loving while Louise still feels constrained?
questions.answer: The story distinguishes kindness from the imposition of another person’s will. Louise’s imagined independence does not require the claim that Brently is openly cruel.

questions.text: How does Josephine misread what Louise is experiencing upstairs?
questions.answer: She fears that Louise is making herself ill behind the closed door. The reader, unlike Josephine, has access to Louise’s thoughts about a newly independent future.

questions.text: What fact overturns the reported railway death?
questions.answer: Brently returns home, unaware of the accident and having been far from it. His ordinary arrival destroys the future Louise has just imagined.

questions.text: Why is the doctors’ explanation of a fatal joy ironic rather than an unquestionable account of Louise’s thoughts?
questions.answer: The doctors see her collapse but do not know her private sense of liberation. Readers may interpret her death as connected to losing that imagined freedom; the story does not provide a medical diagnosis proving the interpretation.
